children: By Kit Norton
It didn't take long for Wall Street to come back around on Amazon.com.
The tech giant's shares jumped Monday as its unstoppable cloud business overshadowed other concerns from its earnings report last week.

Amazon stock rose 4.2% to $250.36 and was on pace to snap a two-day losing streak after declining 3% following earnings. Those third-quarter earnings on Thursday came in below expectations on the back of ailing revenue from retail and advertising.

But Phillip Securities analyst Helena Wang on Monday upgraded Amazon stock to Buy from Accumulate and raised her price target to $330 from $320. That new price target represented 37% upside from the closing price of $240.35 on Friday.
The basis for the upgrade was that Amazon Web Services, the company's cloud business, is expected to continue growing at a strong pace.

"We think AMZN is well-positioned in AI by being model-agnostic and leveraging its full-stack capabilities, including custom chips and partnerships with large language models," Wang said in the research note.
The analyst added that while "aggressive" capital spending does create some free cash flow pressure, Amazon's "strong demand visibility supports sustained infrastructure investment."
"We believe these investments will benefit AMZN over the long term, strengthen its market leadership and create significant barriers to entry for potential competitors," Wang said.
Wang's optimistic take on Amazon was only the latest example that Wall Street was looking for the positives out of Amazon's earnings.

What stole the bulk of the headlines last week was that the online retailer-and-cloud computing provider disclosed that its free cash flow was negative $42.4 billion for the 12 months ending in September as the costs of its artificial-intelligence data center buildout soared.
That was quite the reversal from the $14.8 billion in cash it generated in the same period a year earlier.

AWS, even so, has been chugging right along. Revenue from AWS grew 39% to $46 billion in the third quarter. Amazon said it believes AWS can boost revenue "north of 40%" each year in 2027 and 2028 and be a "trillion-dollar revenue business" in five to 10 years.
Wall Street was choosing to focus on that positive.
Mizuho Securities on Friday raised its Amazon stock price target to $350 from $330 and maintained an Outperform rating on the shares.

"We remain constructive on the AWS story, with the company well positioned as inference demand defuses, open source models proliferate, and with wide frontier model availability on AWS," the firm said.
Mizuho added that while there are "legitimate near-term concerns around capital intensity," the acceleration in AWS is hard to underestimate.

Morgan Stanley analyst Brian Nowak on Friday also sounded an optimistic tone on AWS even as he reduced his Amazon stock price target to $335 from $350. Nowak maintained an Overweight rating on the shares.
"We continue to think AWS's ability to reach $1 trillion in revenue and $500 billion in earnings before interest and taxes is not priced in at current levels," Nowak said in the research note.
The analyst added that AWS's business growth potential is "likely to put higher floors in earnings power going forward."
Suffice it to say that even as free cash flow and AI spending might be a concern, Wall Street has made it clear it likes AWS too much to be overly concerned.
